title: Transplant Viral Loads: CMV Resistance Genes, BK Nephropathy and Integrated HHV-6
summary: Read three transplant viral loads correctly: when refractory CMV needs UL97 and UL54 genotyping and what each resistance gene means, how plasma BK virus screening and thresholds define probable and presumptive nephropathy, and why a huge stable HHV-6 load may be inherited chromosomal integration.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 64 Hit 5 (CMV resistance genes), Hit 9 (BK virus nephropathy) and Exam Trap 5 (high HHV-6 load and inherited integration). Checked against the Fourth International CMV SOT guidelines (Kotton 2025), the Second International BK guidelines (Kotton 2024), Alsanea 2024 and Pellett 2012. Hit 5’s “UL54 = high-level ganciclovir + foscarnet/cidofovir cross-resistance” is qualified: cross-resistance is mutation-specific, high-level ganciclovir resistance can result from UL97 plus UL54 mutations combined, and maribavir resistance also maps to UL97 (register flag rv-cmv-ul54-crossres). Hit 9 (“up to 15%”) matches the guideline range (about 8%, range 1–15%, first year). Trap 5’s “<1%” is given by Pellett 2012 as about 1% (higher in some patient groups). Not taught: Number Vault CMV reactivation rates, adenovirus rates, antiviral dosing.

objectives: Name the CMV genes linked to ganciclovir, foscarnet/cidofovir, maribavir and letermovir resistance and when genotyping is indicated.
Apply plasma BK virus screening intervals and the probable and presumptive BK nephropathy thresholds.
Recognise when a very high, stable HHV-6 load suggests inherited chromosomally integrated HHV-6 rather than active infection.

scenes.title: Three transplant viral loads
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Three transplant recipients with quantitative PCR results: (1) kidney recipient, month 4, plasma BK virus DNA 25,000 copies/mL; (2) liver recipient, CMV DNAemia that has not fallen after 3 weeks of full-dose valganciclovir, on top of earlier prophylaxis; (3) heart recipient, well, with HHV-6 DNA above 1 million copies/mL of whole blood on every sample for months. Question token: “Which number means what?”

cues.text: Three transplant recipients, three quantitative viral loads.

A kidney recipient with plasma BK virus at twenty-five thousand copies. A liver recipient whose CMV load has not fallen after three weeks of full-dose treatment. A well heart recipient with HHV-6 above a million copies in every blood sample.
Which number means disease, which means drug resistance, and which may not be infection at all?

scenes.title: Why transplant labs count virus
scenes.altText: Context cards (Kotton 2025 CMV; Kotton 2024 BK; Pellett 2012). CMV: DNAemia is monitored weekly during treatment with an assay calibrated to the WHO standard. BK polyomavirus: no established vaccine or effective antiviral, so kidney recipients are screened for plasma BK DNA monthly to month 9, then every 3 months to 2 years; biopsy-proven BK nephropathy affects about 8% (range 1–15%) in the first year. HHV-6: about 1% of people in US and UK studies carry the whole HHV-6 genome integrated into a chromosome telomere, inherited through the germline, so every nucleated cell is presumed to carry at least one copy.

cues.text: Transplant labs measure viral loads because immunosuppression lets latent viruses replicate. For CMV, the load is followed weekly during treatment, using an assay calibrated to the WHO standard.
BK polyomavirus has no established vaccine or effective antiviral. So kidney recipients are screened for plasma BK DNA monthly until month nine, then every three months until two years.
In the first year after transplant, biopsy-proven BK nephropathy occurs in about eight percent of kidney recipients, with a range of one to fifteen percent.
HHV-6 is different. In US and UK studies, about one percent of people inherit the whole HHV-6 genome built into a chromosome, so every nucleated cell is presumed to carry a copy.

props.title: Integrated HHV-6 (~1%)
lines: A copy in every nucleated cell

scenes.title: CMV resistance genes and when to test
scenes.altText: Gene cards (Kotton 2025; Alsanea 2024). UL97 kinase: phosphorylates ganciclovir; after ganciclovir or valganciclovir, UL97 mutations appear first in about 90% of cases; the usual ganciclovir mutations (codons 460, 520, 590–607) do not affect foscarnet or cidofovir. UL97 is also the site of maribavir resistance (T409M, H411Y). UL54 DNA polymerase: usually later, adds ganciclovir resistance and may cross-resist cidofovir and/or foscarnet depending on the mutation; foscarnet and cidofovir resistance arises only from UL54; UL97 plus UL54 together can give high-level (20–30-fold) ganciclovir resistance. UL56 terminase: letermovir; codon 325 mutations give absolute resistance; low-grade mutations also in UL89 and UL51. When to test: refractory infection after at least 2 weeks of properly dosed therapy plus cumulative exposure of 4 weeks or more; results more reliable at a load of at least 1000 IU/mL; routinely sequence UL97 and UL54, add UL56 after letermovir.

cues.text: CMV drug resistance lives in a few genes. UL97, the viral kinase, phosphorylates ganciclovir. After ganciclovir, UL97 mutations appear first in about ninety percent of cases, and the usual ones leave foscarnet and cidofovir working.

UL54, the DNA polymerase, usually mutates later. It adds ganciclovir resistance and, depending on the mutation, can cross-resist cidofovir or foscarnet. UL97 plus UL54 together can give high-level resistance.
UL56, part of the terminase, is the main letermovir resistance gene. And maribavir resistance maps back to UL97.

Suspect resistance when the load fails to fall after two weeks of properly dosed therapy, with four or more weeks of total drug exposure. Genotyping is most reliable with at least one thousand IU per mL, and should routinely cover UL97 and UL54.

scenes.title: Read the three numbers
scenes.altText: Decision cards. (1) BK: plasma BK DNA >10,000 copies/mL on one sample = presumptive BK nephropathy; >1000 copies/mL sustained >2 weeks = probable; the main treatment is reducing immunosuppression; biopsy confirmation uses immunohistochemistry for large T antigen with an SV40 cross-reacting antibody. (2) CMV: refractory after 3 weeks of proper dosing with more than 4 weeks of total exposure → genotype UL97 and UL54 (most reliable when the sample has ≥1000 IU/mL). (3) HHV-6: whole-blood loads usually above 1 million genomes/mL and a viral-to-human genome ratio near 1:1 suggest inherited chromosomally integrated HHV-6; hair-follicle or nail PCR can confirm; screening may prevent unnecessary antivirals. Serum can read up to 100-fold higher than plasma because clotting lyses cells.

cues.text: Patient one: plasma BK virus above ten thousand copies on a single sample means presumptive BK nephropathy. Above one thousand sustained for more than two weeks is probable. The main treatment is reducing immunosuppression.
Patient two: three weeks of proper dosing, more than four weeks of total exposure, and a load that will not fall. That is refractory CMV, so send it for UL97 and UL54 genotyping.

Patient three: HHV-6 above a million per mL, unchanged for months, in a well patient. Suspect inherited integrated HHV-6. A viral-to-human genome ratio near one to one, or HHV-6 DNA in hair follicles, supports it.
Recognising integration may prevent unnecessary antiviral treatment. And note that serum can read up to a hundred-fold higher than plasma, because clotting breaks open cells.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “High HHV-6 load in a transplant patient = active infection, treat” (✓ about 1% have inherited integrated HHV-6, with a copy in every cell; check the clinical picture and the viral-to-cell ratio); “A UL97 mutation means foscarnet and cidofovir will fail too” (✓ usual UL97 ganciclovir mutations spare foscarnet and cidofovir; resistance to those arises in UL54); “CMV load rising in week 1 of treatment = resistance” (✓ not predictive; suspect resistance after ≥2 weeks of proper dosing and ≥4 weeks of total exposure).

cues.text: Trap one: a high HHV-6 load in a transplant patient means active infection. No: inherited integration gives a copy in every cell, so read the patient and the ratio, not the number.
Trap two: a UL97 mutation means foscarnet and cidofovir will fail too. No: the usual UL97 mutations spare them. Resistance to those drugs comes from UL54.
Trap three: a CMV load that rises in the first week means resistance. No: early rises are not predictive. Test after two weeks of proper dosing.

props.title: ✗ “UL97 = foscarnet and cidofovir fail.”
lines: ✓ Usual UL97 mutations spare them; UL54 may not

props.title: ✗ “Week-1 rise = resistance.”
lines: ✓ Test after ≥ 2 wk proper dosing, ≥ 4 wk total

scenes.title: 97 opens, 54 piles on, 56 locks letermovir
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “97 OPENS the door (kinase, ganciclovir resistance first); 54 PILES ON (polymerase, can add cidofovir and foscarnet); 56 LOCKS letermovir (terminase). BK counts in thousands: above 1,000 for more than 2 weeks is probable, 10,000 is presumptive. Integrated HHV-6 is a CENSUS, not a fire: about one copy per cell.” Tokens: 97 first · 54 piles on · 56 letermovir. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: ninety-seven opens the door, the kinase, ganciclovir first. Fifty-four piles on, the polymerase that can add cidofovir and foscarnet. Fifty-six locks letermovir. And integrated HHV-6 is a census, not a fire: about one copy per cell.

Where it breaks: cross-resistance depends on the exact mutation; maribavir resistance also sits in UL97; low-grade letermovir resistance can involve other terminase genes; and integrated HHV-6 may possibly be reactivated, which is not yet proven in patients.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “CMV refractory ≥2 weeks → genotype UL97 + UL54 · UL56 for letermovir”, “BK plasma >10,000 copies/mL = presumptive nephropathy · stable huge HHV-6 load → think integration”.

cues.text: In transplant virology a viral load must be read in context, because CMV that will not fall after two weeks of proper therapy needs UL97 and UL54 genotyping, plasma BK virus above 10,000 copies per mL signals presumptive nephropathy, and a very high but stable HHV-6 load may be inherited chromosomal integration rather than active infection.

props.label: CMV refractory ≥ 2 wk → UL97 + UL54 · UL56 for letermovir
BK > 10,000 = presumptive · huge stable HHV-6 → integration

explanation.what: Plain language: after a transplant, drugs that stop rejection also weaken defences against viruses that hide in the body. Labs count how much virus is in blood. For CMV, a count that will not fall on treatment can mean the virus has mutated to escape the drug. For BK virus, a rising count warns that the new kidney is being damaged. For HHV-6, a huge count can simply mean the person was born with the virus’s genes built into every cell. Scientific terms: CMV DNAemia, genotypic resistance testing, UL97 kinase, UL54 DNA polymerase, UL56 terminase, refractory CMV infection, BK polyomavirus DNAemia, probable and presumptive BK nephropathy, decoy cells, inherited chromosomally integrated HHV-6.
explanation.why: Ganciclovir needs UL97 to phosphorylate it, so kinase mutations are the usual first escape; foscarnet and cidofovir act on the polymerase, so their resistance arises in UL54. BK has no established effective antiviral, so early detection by plasma screening allows reduction of immunosuppression before major graft damage. Integrated HHV-6 sits in every nucleated cell, so the DNA load tracks cell number, not replication.
explanation.measure: CMV: suspect resistance after ≥2 weeks of properly dosed therapy with ≥4 weeks of cumulative exposure; genotyping is more reliable when the specimen has ≥1000 IU/mL; sequence UL97 and UL54 routinely, UL56 after letermovir. BK: plasma screening monthly to month 9, then every 3 months to 2 years; >1000 copies/mL for >2 weeks = probable, >10,000 copies/mL = presumptive nephropathy; reduce immunosuppression. HHV-6: whole-blood loads usually >1 million genomes/mL with a viral-to-human genome ratio about 1:1; hair-follicle or nail PCR can confirm; serum may be ~100-fold higher than plasma.
explanation.differs: UL97 (ganciclovir first, usual mutations spare foscarnet/cidofovir; also maribavir) vs UL54 (later, possible multidrug resistance) vs UL56 (letermovir); refractory infection vs proven drug resistance; BK screening (urine decoy cells, high negative predictive value) vs plasma BK DNA (better positive predictive value); integrated HHV-6 vs active HHV-6 infection.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which gene explains which drug failure, when to order CMV genotyping, BK nephropathy thresholds and first-line management, and the high-HHV-6-load trap in a well transplant patient.

mnemonic.text: 97 OPENS the door (kinase, ganciclovir resistance first); 54 PILES ON (polymerase, can add cidofovir and foscarnet); 56 LOCKS letermovir (terminase). Integrated HHV-6 is a CENSUS, not a fire: about one copy per cell.
mnemonic.explanation: Encodes the order and drug targets of the main CMV resistance genes and why integrated HHV-6 loads are high.
mnemonic.limitation: Cross-resistance depends on the exact mutation; maribavir resistance also maps to UL97; low-grade letermovir resistance has also been mapped to UL89 and UL51; integrated HHV-6 might be induced to reactivate (shown in cultured cells).

analogyLimitations: Thresholds are assay-dependent; guidelines give BK values in copies/mL “or equivalent”.
Gene–drug patterns are simplified; real interpretation uses the phenotype of each specific mutation.
takeaway: In transplant virology a viral load must be read in context, because CMV that will not fall after two weeks of proper therapy needs UL97 and UL54 genotyping, plasma BK virus above 10,000 copies per mL signals presumptive nephropathy, and a very high but stable HHV-6 load may be inherited chromosomal integration rather than active infection.

questions.stem: A liver transplant recipient with refractory CMV has a genotype showing a single UL97 M460V mutation and wild-type UL54. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Ganciclovir resistance, with foscarnet and cidofovir susceptibility usually preserved
options.rationale: Correct. The usual UL97 ganciclovir mutations do not affect foscarnet or cidofovir, which act on the UL54 polymerase.

options.text: Letermovir resistance, because UL97 is the terminase gene
options.rationale: Incorrect. Letermovir resistance mainly maps to the UL56 terminase gene; UL97 is the kinase.

options.text: Foscarnet resistance, because all UL97 mutations cross-resist foscarnet
options.rationale: Incorrect. Foscarnet and cidofovir resistance arises in UL54, not UL97.

options.text: No resistance, because only UL54 mutations affect ganciclovir
options.rationale: Incorrect. UL97 mutations are the usual first cause of ganciclovir resistance.

questions.stem: Four months after kidney transplantation, a recipient without rejection has plasma BK polyomavirus DNA of 15,000 copies/mL on a screening sample. What does this indicate and what is the main management step?

options.text: Presumptive BK nephropathy; reduce maintenance immunosuppression
options.rationale: Correct. A single plasma load above 10,000 copies/mL defines presumptive BK nephropathy, and reducing immunosuppression is the primary treatment.

options.text: Normal viruria; no action until decoy cells appear
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is plasma DNAemia, not viruria, and it is above the presumptive threshold.

options.text: Start an established BK antiviral as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Incorrect. The guidelines state no effective BK antivirals are currently established for clinical use.

options.text: Repeat only urine testing, which predicts nephropathy better than plasma
options.rationale: Incorrect. Plasma BK DNA has a higher positive predictive value than high-level urine loads or decoy cells.

questions.stem: A well heart transplant recipient has HHV-6 DNA above 1 million copies/mL of whole blood on every sample for months. Which step best addresses the most likely explanation?

options.text: Assess for inherited chromosomally integrated HHV-6, for example by viral-to-human genome ratio or hair-follicle PCR
options.rationale: Correct. A ratio near one viral copy per cell, or HHV-6 DNA in hair follicles, supports inherited integration and can prevent unnecessary antivirals.

options.text: Start antiviral therapy for active HHV-6 infection immediately
options.rationale: Incorrect. Integrated HHV-6 gives persistently very high loads on its own; antivirals might be warranted only for a compatible illness with other causes excluded.

options.text: Retest on serum, which removes cellular DNA
options.rationale: Incorrect. Clotting lyses cells, so serum HHV-6 DNA can be up to 100-fold higher than plasma.

options.text: Report the result as laboratory contamination
options.rationale: Incorrect. A reproducible high load over months fits integration, not contamination.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 64 Hit 5 states UL54 polymerase mutations give high-level ganciclovir plus foscarnet/cidofovir cross-resistance. Kotton 2025 says UL54 mutations add ganciclovir resistance and likely/may cross-resist cidofovir and/or foscarnet depending on the mutation; high-level (20–30-fold) ganciclovir resistance can result from UL97 plus UL54 mutations combined; maribavir resistance also maps to UL97, and low-grade letermovir resistance mutations have also been found in UL51/UL89 besides UL56 (register flag rv-cmv-ul54-crossres).
